body.text: In 2012 a Canadian man named Dennis Meads walked into an Alberta courtroom carrying a stack of papers he believed would change his life. Change was needed. Dennis was in the middle of a difficult divorce that already had him emotionally and financially reeling. Like many before him, Dennis believed he had a silver bullet that would solve all his problems. His optimism was not informed by the services of a lawyer; instead, Dennis was brimming with the secret knowledge his “sovereign citizen” teachers had promised would work.

The advice he carried came straight from the sovereign playbook. To Dennis, the courtroom was less a place of justice than a trap run by corporations masquerading as governments. The solution, his teachers assured him, was simple: assert his “sovereignty” by invoking the right words, the right documents, the right phrases.

He claimed the court had no jurisdiction over him because he was not the legal “person” named in the proceedings but a “living man.” He impugned the validity of the court by arguing that it was an “admiralty court” with jurisdiction on water but not over a “freeman on the land.” He insisted the rules of Canadian family law didn’t apply to him. He piled up contracts, affidavits and pseudolegal declarations written in language that looked impressive. He filed a power of attorney in which “DENNIS LARRY MEADS grants general authority to Dennis-Larry: Meads,” a fee schedule, and a Uniform Commercial Code search of “DENNIS LARRY MEADS, foreign situs cestui que vie trust.” If he was going to bother turning up to this corrupt court, he might as well make it worth his while.
Alongside these (and other) assorted documents, he filed notices seeking C$100 billion, or the equivalent in silver and gold, from the Bank of Canada.

The judge in the case, Associate Chief Justice John Rooke, had seen this sort of thing before. In fact, he had seen it too many times. Rather than simply dismissing these submissions — and faintly hoping they would not return to his courtroom — Judge Rooke sought to understand and dispel this type of argument once and for all. A key insight from Rooke was that these emerging legal arguments were not spreading randomly. Instead, they were organised, packaged and sold. The entrepreneurial “gurus,” as Rooke called them, had built an industry around grievance. They promised salvation in the form of prepared scripts, handbooks, DVDs and webinars, a new medium for dispersal in the early 2010s. Every sentence was marketed as a tool of empowerment. Every affidavit was a product.

Like fast food or Hollywood movies, this type of conspiracy-laden legality proved an easy commodity to export. By the time Judge Rooke identified the various threads as involving “Organised Pseudolegal Commercial Arguments,” it had already travelled well beyond its native United States.

In Canada, men in cowboy hats strode into courtrooms and declared that they stood outside the reach of government jurisdiction. In New Zealand, individuals facing council rate increases scrawled strange symbols on envelopes, insisting that only “living men” could be taxed. In Namibia, one man upset about being sacked from his job filed a claim declaring that he was a “non-corporate citizen, non-civilly dead entity citizen.” Each scene was parochial, rooted in its own moment of frustration, drawing on local legal discourse, and yet each also drew on the same overarching/underlying script. As the Namibian judge in that case noted, the plaintiff had “without a doubt” copied his claims from the internet.

What united the Canadian cowboys, New Zealand rate payers and Namibian job seekers — and still does — is a conviction that the system is rigged. They are not wrong to feel that way. Modern legal systems favour the wealthy and powerful; access to justice is expensive, and ordinary people routinely feel steamrolled by bureaucracy and banks. When the law allows massive corporations to avoid liability and tax through clever legal manoeuvres, when it permits the great and the mighty to silence critics by threatening expensive litigation, when it feels like big banks have more rights than real people, it is no wonder that regular people lose hope. Some people try to find out what happened to the society they grew up in. They may even try to use the same tactics they see big corporations get away with — like attempting to rely on corporate personality to avoid registering their dog or vehicle.

Corporate personality is the idea that corporations are, in law, persons, separate from their owners, managers and agents. This foundational legal principle is a cornerstone of modern business. It allows corporations to hold property, enter contracts, and sue and be sued like a natural person. By ensuring that the corporation is responsible for its debts and actions, corporate personality promotes investment and reduces personal risk for business owners.

But it can also allow individuals to shield themselves from personal liability for wrongdoing they might have committed in the company’s name. It is all well and good to sue a corporation, but as Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain Edward Thurlow famously observed in the late eighteenth century, “corporations have neither bodies to be punished, nor souls to be condemned.” Here, as in many other ways, pseudolaw repackages real insights about the harmful aspects of our law with a “hidden history” that explains how a shadowy cabal has taken over the state.

The genius — and the cruelty — of pseudolaw lies in commodification. Desperate people, often facing foreclosure, divorce or tax bills, are transformed into customers. For a few hundred dollars, they can attend a seminar in a hotel ballroom. For a small website subscription fee, they can join an online community that offers templates to cancel debts or “reclaim sovereignty” as a natural person. The ideology has been repackaged as a kit you can buy, a do-it-yourself escape hatch from your problems. It has spread everywhere, from radio broadcasts to hotels, from prisons to social media, and, of course, to online booksellers. A cursory scan of Amazon’s website reveals a treasure trove of SovCit materials. Anyone aggrieved is a potential buyer.

The product gurus sell — legal misinformation — is largely the same. But different gurus offer slightly different variations. Just as Colgate sells more than forty different types of toothpaste — from cavity protection, to whitening, to sensitivity — gurus dress the same basic ingredients in different packaging.

The austere and serious guru might emphasise a bewildering linguistics that aims to confuse and overwhelm; a gentler-looking guru might adopt a folksy approach to commerce that seeks to draw in the down-to-earth. More modern gurus follow the zeitgeist, marinating their product in irony and crude humour. Marketing appeals to those already inclined toward the message or who recognise something in it, turning them into buyers and then, quite literally, investors. Pseudolaw, in other words, is not only a conspiracy theory. It is an industry. It thrives because grievance is universal. And business is booming.

As these legal conspiracies initially began to migrate from the United States, judges did not know what to make of it — it was “incomprehensible,” “nonsense” or “gobbledygook.” It was nonsense, that is, until Dennis Meads walked into that Alberta courtroom. To a layperson, the arguments he presented might have seemed bewildering, maybe even clever, like some obscure trick that lawyers didn’t want ordinary people to know. But to Associate Chief Justice John Rooke, they were worse than meaningless. They represented the increasingly burdensome toil of “nonsense” litigation that had become far too familiar. Instead of simply dismissing the case, like the many he had before, he decided to take action.

What followed was a judgement that went far beyond Dennis’s divorce proceedings. Having reviewed more than 160 cases, Judge Rooke issued a decision spanning more than 700 paragraphs and 180 pages. It reads less like a ruling on spousal support payments than an encyclopedia of legal conspiracy theories in Canada. He carefully dissected the arguments, tracing them back to American tax protest movements and sovereign citizen groups, noting where distinct Canadian pseudolegal tropes had emerged. He showed that these schemes were not new, and that they never succeeded.

Judge Rooke identified the commercial side of the movement. Systemically reviewing the phenomenon through hundreds of cases, he recognised that Dennis was engaging in a familiar pattern, speaking from a script that he’d altered to fit his circumstances. Often, these claimants were using the same templates with new content placed in them. The same key figures, “gurus,” kept appearing. He identified them by their “advocacy” and their hallmark innovations. Rooke called these ideas “Organized Pseudolegal Commercial Arguments.”

For Dennis Meads, the immediate consequences were devastating. His attempt to escape family court obligations and evade the court’s jurisdiction collapsed, leaving him where he began — still embroiled in a messy divorce, still subject to Canadian law. But while the divorce proceedings dragged on for another five slow, circuitous years, Judge Rooke’s comprehensive findings convinced Meads to abandon the gurus. He even turned to a real lawyer for help.

The case has left a far broader legacy than pulling Dennis out of the rabbit hole he found himself in (and sparing his ex-partner and their children further hassle). It marked the moment when Canadian courts developed the vocabulary to describe the phenomenon that sovereign citizens were spreading around the globe. These strange forms of argument and curious language became known as pseudolaw.

It was a landmark. In the same way that Canadian courts began citing Meads v Meads whenever pseudolaw appeared, judges in Australia, the United Kingdom, New Zealand and elsewhere referenced it too. It became a rare example of a “rock-star” decision, read widely by judges and the public. One magazine even described it as possessing a “cult following.” Meads is a global manual for how to identify, name and respond to pseudolegal contests.

Giving a name to the phenomenon enables us to track it. We can note different iterations and evaluate how it evolves as it travels across the globe. It means that we can “see” it when it turns up in court, when it is argued at traffic stops, and when it turns violent. But telling believers that they are using fake or ersatz law does not faze (most of) them. Their losses merely confirm how corrupt the state is.

Pseudolaw spreads so well because individuals who are drowning in debt and searching for an out will take any available option. Citizens who feel cheated by the government don’t want to pay for services that they feel do not directly benefit them. If aggrieved individuals are willing to pay for a script to follow or someone to help support them in court, the psychological hook can be devastating.

Families lose homes because instead of working with a lawyer or with a bank to restructure their loans, they trust that pseudolaw can allow them to opt out of mortgages entirely. Parents lose custody battles because they file meaningless documents instead of complying with court orders. In some cases, using pseudolaw has been upheld as an indication that the parent is unfit to look after their child. Instead of relying on qualified defence counsel, individuals are jailed for contempt after shouting pseudolegal slogans in courtrooms.

Judge Rooke’s decision in Meads was an effort to slow the spread of pseudolegal discourse. But naming the phenomenon has not stopped it. Pseudolaw is not just bad law or misinformation. It is a business. But if it doesn’t work, then how does this business continue to survive? What is that consumers are actually buying? •
This is an edited extract from Outlawed: Responding to the Global Rise of Sovereign Citizens and Legal Conspiracies, by Harry Hobbs and Stephen Young, published last month by Penguin.
